newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - E. Europe bourses drift, eye new issues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - E. Europe bourses drift, eye new issues.

text.p: East European shares moved mostly sideways in light trade this week, with business in several centres dampened by upcoming new share issues, and Bucharest was the only market to record strong gains and higher volumes.
Warsaw and Budapest rose, Bucharest hit all-time highs in record volumes, Croatian stocks traded mixed, while Prague, Bratislava and Ljubljana shares edged lower in thin volumes.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 73 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, edged a little higher through the week.
WARSAW

The Warsaw bourse gained 3.6 percent this week, buoyed by generally good March earnings and lower-than-expected inflation data, with analysts expecting low inflation forecasts to keep the market mood positive.
But apart from construction firms buoyed by good earnings prospects ahead of the summer season, traders saw few bargains and little room for growth for the overall market.

"Most stocks seem fairly valued or slightly expensive but there's not a big potential for falls," said Roman Sosnowski of Bank Staropolski brokerage, who said the bourse could stay in a channel between 16,000 and 17,000 points.
Analysts said the busy primary market schedule could also dampen buying in coming sessions.
PRAGUE
The Czech PX50 index edged lower in very thin trade.
Despite a brief upturn in the middle of last week after the government vowed to tighten capital market regulation, dealers said the market mood was bearish and lethargic with little foreign activity.
"Blue chips are almost dead and second-tier stocks almost illiquid," said Radim Bajgar of ING Barings.
BUDAPEST

Hungarian shares edged higher this week after Monday's 3.5 percent rally but the market remained in a broader sideways trend with investors waiting for new share offers and first-quarter earnings reports.
"We'll know the underlying trend when the first-quarter figures are released and when share offers are completed," said Gabor Sitanyi, analyst at ING Barings in London.
Oil company MOL was in focus this week and traders said MOL shares were bought mainly by domestic investors.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks traded mixed throughout the week and traders saw stabilisation following a recent bullish trend set off by blue chip gains.
Zagrebacka Banka ordinary share hit an all-time high on Tuesday, lifted by strong 1996 results, and kept rising to close at 2,215 kuna on Thursday.
Blue-chip drug maker Pliva gained 20 kuna since Tuesday to close at 480 and traders saw room for more gains following its recent strong 1996 report.
Food stock Podravka resisted the Thursday lull, trading in large volumes at an unchanged 305 kuna.
Varazdinska banka was expected to get a boost from a Thursday vote on a 160-to-1 stock split.
BRATISLAVA

A lack of offers brought trading near to a standstill over the week with the 16-share official SAX index hovering around last week's level and closing at 194.54 points on Thursday, just down from Monday's opening.
Brokers saw no signs of change in the near future.
"The market has not been supplied with any significantly positive information which might perhaps wake up some currently inactive issues," Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said.
Steel maker VSZ remained virtually the only liquid blue chip, closing 10 crowns up at 740 crowns on Thursday.
BUCHAREST
A bull run this week boosted volumes and sent two independent indices to consecutive year highs.
The highlight of the week was a special deal in high-cap Azomures fertiliser maker, which drove turnover to a record high of 25.73 billion lei, or five times the previous level.
Traders saw foreign interest behind the Azomures special trade -- a large deal struck outside the market. Azomures rose 400 lei to 2,500 following the deal.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares eased 1.9 percent this week with turnover down to 176.6 million tolars from 291.4 million.
Pharmaceutical wholesaler Salus led the week's decliners, falling 12.6 percent, while preferred shares of bank UBK were the top gainer, firming 1.63 percent.
Traders said stagnation would continue until foreign capital returned to the market as domestic investors lacked funds to support steady growth on the market that expects new listings next month.
